chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Board, the Auditor and the Pay Packet

lessons.title: Managerial Remuneration: Is Pay Linked to Performance?

body.text: Pay is where management's interests are written down in rupees. Read it to find out who the company is really being run for.

children.text: In most large Western companies, the CEO is a hired professional and shareholders worry about overpaying an employee. In India there is a second, bigger issue: the highest-paid executives are often the promoter and their family members, who also control the board that approves their pay. Remuneration then stops being only a cost question and becomes a minority shareholder question. Every rupee of excess pay to a promoter-executive is profit that comes out before dividends are shared with you.
You do not need to decide what a fair salary is. You need to answer three questions: how big is the pay relative to the company, how is it structured, and does it move with performance?
The Rules That Cap and Expose Pay

body.caption: Key remuneration rules for Indian listed companies

cells: Overall cap
Total managerial remuneration to all directors and the manager is capped at 11% of net profits, calculated as per Section 198
Companies Act, 2013, Section 197
Individual caps
One managing director or whole-time director: up to 5% of net profits; if there is more than one, up to 10% together. Non-executive directors: up to 1% if there is an MD or WTD, otherwise 3%
Companies Act, 2013, Section 197
Exceeding the caps

Allowed with shareholder approval by special resolution. If the company has defaulted on dues to banks or other lenders, their prior approval is needed. Loss-making companies follow the limits in Schedule V
Companies Act, 2013, Section 197 and Schedule V
Promoter-executives

Special resolution needed if a promoter or promoter group executive director's annual pay exceeds ₹5 crore or 2.5% of net profits, whichever is higher; or if pay to all such directors together exceeds 5% of net profits
LODR Regulation 17(6)(e)
Relatives on the payroll
A director's or KMP's relative holding an office or place of profit with monthly pay above ₹2.5 lakh needs shareholder approval as a related party transaction
Companies Act, 2013, Section 188 and rules
Disclosure
Ratio of each director's pay to median employee pay, percentage increase for each director and KMP, and the increase in median employee pay, with justification
Companies Act, 2013, Section 197(12) and Rule 5(1)

body.text: A special resolution needs 75% of votes cast. A promoter with 55% cannot pass one alone, so large pay packages for promoter-executives need real support from minority shareholders. That makes the AGM voting results on pay resolutions one of the clearest measures of what independent investors think of management.

children.text: Question 1: How Big Is the Pay?

Absolute numbers mean little on their own. A ₹20 crore package is modest at a company earning ₹5,000 crore and extraordinary at one earning ₹150 crore. Use three yardsticks, all of which you can calculate from the annual report.

body.latex: \text{Pay to Profit} = \frac{\text{Executive Pay}}{\text{Net Profit}} \times 100 \qquad \text{Pay Ratio} = \frac{\text{Executive Pay}}{\text{Median Employee Pay}}
body.caption: Use reported net profit as a quick approximation; the legal limits use net profit calculated under Section 198
Three yardsticks for the size of pay

cells: Pay to profit
Each executive's pay and all executive pay combined, divided by net profit
Any single executive above 5%, or promoter family members together taking a large and rising share
Pay ratio
Disclosed directly in the Board's Report as the ratio to median employee remuneration
A ratio far above sector peers, or rising quickly while median pay barely moves
Peer comparison
Compare pay to profit and pay ratio with two or three listed competitors of similar size
Pay far above peers without clearly superior returns on capital

body.title: Calculate the Pay Ratio
body.prompt: A company's managing director earned total remuneration of ₹18 crore last year. The median employee earned ₹6 lakh. What is the ratio of the MD's pay to median employee pay?
body.explanation: ₹18 crore = ₹1,800 lakh. ₹1,800 lakh ÷ ₹6 lakh = 300. The MD earns 300 times the median employee. The number alone does not prove overpayment, but you should compare it with peers and, more importantly, with how the ratio has moved as profits changed.

children.text: Question 2: How Is the Pay Structured?

Pay in Indian companies is typically made up of fixed salary and perquisites, a performance bonus or variable pay, commission calculated as a percentage of profits, and for professional managers, stock options. Promoters are not eligible for ESOPs under SEBI's share-based employee benefit rules, and independent directors cannot receive them either, so for promoter-executives the mix of fixed pay and profit commission is what you are really reading.

columns.label: Aligned With Shareholders
points: A meaningful share of pay is variable and falls in bad years
Variable pay tied to disclosed targets such as ROCE, EPS growth, or cash flow
Commission on profits capped at a fixed amount
Professional managers hold ESOPs that vest over several years
Promoter pay cut or waived voluntarily when profits fall

columns.label: Extractive
points: Mostly fixed pay that rises every year regardless of results
Commission on profits that include one-off gains such as asset sales
Several family members on the payroll as executive directors or in senior roles
Additional pay drawn from subsidiaries, making the parent's disclosure look smaller
Minimum remuneration sought through special resolutions in loss-making years

body.text: Always look for pay drawn from subsidiaries. Under Section 197(14), a managing director or whole-time director receiving commission from the company can also receive pay from a holding or subsidiary company, as long as it is disclosed in the Board's Report. Add it all up before judging the total.

children.text: Question 3: Does Pay Move With Performance?

This is the question that matters most, and it needs five years of data, not one. Take an illustrative promoter-MD whose pay rose from ₹12 crore to ₹30 crore over five years, while net profit went from ₹400 crore to ₹440 crore and median employee pay rose from ₹6.0 lakh to ₹7.0 lakh. Index all three to 100 in Year 0.

body.title: Promoter-MD pay vs net profit vs median employee pay (indexed, Year 0 = 100)

body.caption: Compare the 5-year CAGR of pay with the 5-year CAGR of profit

children.text: Profit barely moved and fell in two of the five years. Pay rose every single year. This is what pay disconnected from performance looks like, and you can build this chart for any company from five years of annual reports.

body.title: Does It Need a Special Resolution?
body.question: In Year 5 of the illustration, the promoter-MD is paid ₹30 crore and net profit is ₹440 crore. Assume Section 198 net profit is the same as reported profit. Which statement is correct?
options: No special resolution is needed, because ₹30 crore is below the 11% overall cap
A special resolution is needed only under LODR, because pay exceeds ₹5 crore

A special resolution is needed under both the Companies Act, because pay is about 6.8% of profit and above the 5% individual cap, and LODR, because pay exceeds the higher of ₹5 crore and 2.5% of profit (₹11 crore)
No approval is needed, because promoters set their own pay
body.explanation: ₹30 crore ÷ ₹440 crore = 6.82%, above the 5% cap for a single MD under Section 197. Under LODR, 2.5% of ₹440 crore is ₹11 crore, which is higher than ₹5 crore, and ₹30 crore exceeds it. So a special resolution with 75% of votes cast is needed, and minority shareholders get a real say.

children.text: Pay resolutions do fail. In 2014, Tata Motors reported a standalone loss and sought special resolutions to pay minimum remuneration to its executive directors above the limits then allowed for loss-making companies. Minority shareholders voted them down, even though the company was part of one of India's most respected groups. The episode showed that when a special resolution is required, promoter support alone is not enough, and institutional investors are willing to vote against pay in loss years regardless of the group's reputation.

For your own holdings, open the voting results filed on BSE or NSE after each AGM and look at pay-related resolutions. The overall result will usually be a pass. The line to read is how public institutions voted. If a large share of institutions voted against a promoter's pay, proxy advisors have probably flagged it, and their report will usually tell you exactly why.

body.title: The Family Payroll
body.scenario: A family-controlled consumer goods company listed on NSE has net profit of ₹640 crore, roughly flat for five years. Three promoter family members are executive directors: the chairman, his son as MD, and his daughter as a whole-time director. Their combined pay is ₹48 crore, double what it was five years ago. Each receives 2% of net profits as commission on top of a fixed salary. Two other relatives work in senior management on salaries of ₹4 lakh a month. The son also receives ₹6 crore a year from a subsidiary, disclosed in the Board's Report. At the last AGM, 58% of public institutional votes went against the MD's reappointment on the proposed terms.
body.prompt: Evaluate this pay structure against the three questions. What does it tell you about how the company treats minority shareholders?
body.modelAnswer: Size: ₹48 crore is 7.5% of ₹640 crore of profit for three people, and adding the son's ₹6 crore from the subsidiary takes the family's pay from the group to ₹54 crore. Any promoter group pay above 5% of net profits in aggregate needs a special resolution under LODR, so this should have been put to shareholders. Structure: commission is a flat percentage of profits with no targets, so it rises with any profit, including one-offs, and never falls below fixed salary. Two more relatives at ₹4 lakh a month are above the ₹2.5 lakh threshold, so their roles are related party transactions requiring approval. Pay was also partly routed through a subsidiary. Performance: pay doubled while profit stayed flat, so there is no visible link between pay and results. The institutional vote shows independent investors have noticed. Together, this suggests the promoter family treats the company's profits as family income first and shareholder returns second. It is not fraud, but it is steady leakage, and it is a strong reason to check related party transactions and capital allocation just as closely.

body.title: Where to find every remuneration number

cells: Board's Report, annexure on Rule 5 particulars
Ratio of each director's pay to median employee pay, percentage increases for directors and KMP, median pay increase, and justification
Corporate Governance Report
Salary, perquisites, commission, and sitting fees for each director, plus service contract and notice period details
Related party note (Ind AS 24)
Compensation to key managerial personnel and payments to their relatives
AGM notice
Proposed pay terms for appointments and reappointments, including commission formulas and ceilings
Voting results on BSE or NSE
How promoters, public institutions, and public non-institutions voted on each pay resolution

body.title: Audit the Pay at One of Your Holdings
steps: From the Corporate Governance Report, list the total pay of every executive director for the last five years, noting who is from the promoter family
Check the Board's Report for any pay drawn from subsidiaries and add it to the totals
Calculate pay as a percentage of net profit for each executive and for all promoter-executives combined
Note the disclosed ratio to median employee pay and the percentage increase in median pay
Calculate the five-year CAGR of executive pay and of net profit, and compare
Read the commission formula in the latest AGM notice: is it capped, and is it based on targets or simply on profit?
Check the latest AGM voting results for the public institutional vote on any pay or reappointment resolution

body.text: Companies named in this lesson are discussed based on public disclosures and widely reported shareholder votes, for education only. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

points: In India, the highest-paid executives are often promoters who control the board, so pay is a minority shareholder issue, not just a cost issue

Section 197 caps total managerial pay at 11% of net profits and a single MD or WTD at 5%; LODR requires a special resolution for promoter-executive pay above ₹5 crore or 2.5% of net profits, whichever is higher
Judge size with pay to profit, the disclosed ratio to median employee pay, and peer comparison
Aligned pay has capped, target-linked variable components that fall in bad years; extractive pay is fixed, rises regardless of results, and is spread across family members and subsidiaries
The decisive test is five years of pay CAGR against profit CAGR; in the illustration pay grew at 20.1% a year while profit grew at 1.9%
AGM voting results show how public institutions voted on pay, which is often the clearest verdict of independent investors
